parts.latex: In a normal distribution, what is the approximate percentage of scores with a $z$-score less than 1?

solutions.latex:
In a normal distribution, about $68\%$ of scores lie within one standard deviation of the mean, that is $-1 < z < 1$.

The remaining $32\%$ is split equally between the two tails, so $16\%$ of scores have $z > 1$.

Scores with $z < 1$ are all the rest:
$$\begin{aligned} P(z<1) &= 100\% - 16\% \\ &= 84\% \end{aligned}$$
This is option C.

parts.latex:
The marks in a test were normally distributed. The mean mark was 60 and the standard deviation was 15.

What was the percentage of marks higher than 90?

solutions.latex:
Here $\mu = 60$ and $\sigma = 15$.

The $z$-score of 90 is
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{90 - 60}{15} \\ &= 2 \end{aligned}$$
\exfigure{271_q18_s1}

By the empirical rule, $5\%$ of scores lie more than 2 standard deviations from the mean, so half of this is above 90.
$$\dfrac{1}{2} \times 5\% = 2.5\%$$
$$\therefore\ 2.5\% \text{ of marks are higher than } 90.$$

parts.latex:
John recently did a class test in each of three subjects. The class scores on each test were normally distributed.

The table shows the subjects and John's scores as well as the mean and standard deviation of the class scores on each test.

\extable{36_q8_t1}

Relative to the rest of the class, which row of the table below shows John's strongest subject and his weakest subject?

solutions.latex:
To compare scores from different normal distributions, use the $z$-score of each score:
$$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$
where $x$ is John's score, $\mu$ the class mean and $\sigma$ the class standard deviation.

The subject with the largest $z$-score is the one where John is furthest above the class mean, so it is his strongest subject. The subject with the smallest $z$-score is his weakest.

Calculating $z$ for each row of the table gives the largest $z$-score for Commerce and the smallest for French.
$$\therefore\ \text{Strongest subject: Commerce; weakest subject: French}$$
This is option A.

parts.latex:
On a test, Zac’s mark corresponded to a $z$-score of 2. The test scores had a mean of 63 and a standard deviation of 8.

What was Zac’s actual mark on the test?

solutions.latex:
Use the $z$-score formula $z = \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, with $z = 2$, $\mu = 63$ and $\sigma = 8$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= \dfrac{x-63}{8}\\ x-63 &= 16\\ x &= 79 \end{aligned}$$
The answer is D.

parts.latex:
In a particular country, the birth weight of babies is normally distributed with a mean of 3000 grams. It is known that $95\%$ of these babies have a birth weight between 1600 grams and 4400 grams.

One of these babies has a birth weight of 3497 grams. What is the $z$-score of this baby’s birth weight?

solutions.latex:
$95\%$ of values lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean, so
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Standard deviation} &= \dfrac{4400 - 3000}{2} \\ &= 700 \text{ g} \end{aligned}$$
$$\begin{aligned} z\text{-score} &= \dfrac{3497 - 3000}{700} \\ &\approx 0.71 \end{aligned}$$
criteria: Uses $z$-score formula with incorrect standard deviation, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
A particular normal distribution has a mean of 40 and a standard deviation of 5.

Convert a score of 47 from this distribution to a $z$-score.
Calculate the percentage of scores in the distribution that will lie between 38 and 47.
parts.note: Normal probabilities from a z-table (z = -0.4 to 1.4), not by the empirical rule

solutions.latex:
The $z$-score is $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, with $x=47$, $\mu=40$, $\sigma=5$.
$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{47-40}{5} \\ &= 1.4 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ z = 1.4$$

Convert both scores to $z$-scores using $z=\dfrac{x-40}{5}$.
$$\begin{aligned} x=38:\quad z &= \dfrac{38-40}{5} = -0.4 \\ x=47:\quad z &= 1.4 \end{aligned}$$
The table gives the percentage between $z=0$ and $z=a$, and the distribution is symmetrical, so the percentage between $z=-0.4$ and $z=0$ equals that between $z=0$ and $z=0.4$.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Between } z=0 \text{ and } z=1.4 &: 41.92\% \\ \text{Between } z=-0.4 \text{ and } z=0 &: 15.54\% \end{aligned}$$
Add the two parts.
$$\begin{aligned} 41.92 + 15.54 &= 57.46 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{about } 57.46\% \text{ of scores lie between 38 and 47}$$
criteria: Finds the $z$-score of 38 or the table values $41.92$ and $15.54$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Use $z$-scores to determine which student performed best on their English exam, compared to their school cohort.

Lachie did not remember his maths mark but did remember being told he had a $z$-score of $+2$ on the Mathematics exam.

Calculate Lachie's raw maths mark and determine who performed best on their Mathematics exam, compared to their school cohort.

solutions.latex:
Use $z = \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ for each English mark.
$$\begin{aligned} \text{Lachie: } z &= \dfrac{68-68}{8} = 0 \\ \text{Emily: } z &= \dfrac{68-74}{6} = -1 \end{aligned}$$
Lachie's $z$-score is higher, so he is further above his school's average.
$$\therefore\ \text{Lachie performed best in English compared with his cohort}$$

For Lachie, $z = 2$, $\mu = 62$, $\sigma = 9$. Use $x = \mu + z\sigma$.
$$\begin{aligned} x &= 62 + 2\times 9 \\ &= 80 \end{aligned}$$
For Emily, with a mark of $79$, $\mu = 64$, $\sigma = 5$:
$$z = \dfrac{79-64}{5} = 3$$
Emily's $z$-score of $3$ is higher than Lachie's $2$.
$$\therefore\ \text{Lachie's mark was } 80 \text{, and Emily performed best in Mathematics compared with her cohort}$$
criteria: Finds Lachie's mark $80$ or Emily's $z$-score $3$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex:
Kyrie plays in three basketball leagues. He wishes to compare the number of points he scored per game with the number of points per game scored by the other players in the leagues.

The number of points scored in each league are normally distributed. The table shows Kyrie’s scores in each of the leagues he plays in, as well as the mean and standard deviation of the points scored per game in each league.

\exfigure{850_q13_1}

Relative to the rest of the players in each league, which row of the table below shows Kyrie’s strongest performance and his weakest performance?

solutions.latex:
Compare the $z$-scores, $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$, of Kyrie's points in each league.
$$\begin{aligned}\text{School league: } z&=\dfrac{35-25}{10}=1\\\text{NSW league: } z&=\dfrac{28-30}{4}=-0.5\\\text{National league: } z&=\dfrac{20-18}{4}=0.5\end{aligned}$$
Therefore his strongest performance is the School league and his weakest is the NSW league, option C.

parts.latex:
Remy achieved a $z$-score of 2.2 on her latest Geography test.

If the test scores were normally distributed with a mean of 64 and a standard deviation of 5, what was Remy’s actual test mark?

solutions.latex:
Use the $z$-score formula $z = \dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$ and make $x$ the subject.

$$\begin{aligned} x &= \mu + z\sigma \\ &= 64 + 2.2\times 5 \\ &= 75 \end{aligned}$$
Remy's mark was $75$, which is option D.

parts.latex: In a normally distributed set of scores, the mean is 35 and the standard deviation is 3. What percentage of scores lie between 26 and 29?

solutions.latex:
Express 26 and 29 as $z$-scores, using mean $35$ and standard deviation $3$.

$$\begin{aligned} 26 &= 35 - 3\times 3 &&(z=-3)\\ 29 &= 35 - 2\times 3 &&(z=-2) \end{aligned}$$
By the empirical rule, about $95\%$ of scores lie within 2 standard deviations of the mean and about $99.7\%$ lie within 3.

So the percentage between $z=-3$ and $z=-2$ and the same percentage between $z=2$ and $z=3$ together make

$$99.7\% - 95\% = 4.7\%$$
By symmetry, each side has half of this.

$$\dfrac{4.7\%}{2} = 2.35\%$$
$$\therefore\ 2.35\% \text{ of scores lie between 26 and 29.}$$
criteria: Identifies the scores as 3 and 2 standard deviations below the mean, or uses $99.7\%$ and $95\%$, or equivalent merit

parts.latex: Zane achieved a mark of 68/80 for his Biology Assessment task 3 exam. The scores for this exam are normally distributed, with a standard deviation of 3.2% and a mean of 80%. If he wants to perform at the same level in the HSC Trial exam, and the mean increases by 5% and the standard deviation decreases by 2%, what mark must he achieve, to the nearest whole mark, if the exam is out of 70?

solutions.latex:
Zane's mark as a percentage:
$$\dfrac{68}{80} = 85\%$$
His $z$-score on the first exam:
$$z = \dfrac{85-80}{3.2} = 1.5625$$
New mean $=80+5=85\%$ and new standard deviation $=3.2-2=1.2\%$. Keep the same $z$-score.
$$\begin{aligned} 1.5625 &= \dfrac{x-85}{1.2} \\ x &= 86.875\% \end{aligned}$$
Convert to a mark out of 70.
$$\begin{aligned} y &= \dfrac{86.875}{100}\times 70 \\ &= 60.81\ldots \\ &\approx 61 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Zane needs } 61 \text{ out of } 70$$
criteria: Finds the required percentage $86.875\%$, or equivalent merit

6696.stem: After completing a numeracy test ($\%$), Hanna had achieved a $z$-score of $-2$.

parts.latex: How does Hanna's result compare with those of her peers? Explain your answer in terms of the mean and standard deviation.
If the mean test mark was 86 and the standard deviation was 4, calculate Hanna's actual mark.

solutions.latex: A $z$-score of $-2$ means Hanna's mark is 2 standard deviations below the mean.

meta.format_note: Source said 'Hazel's score'; corrected to Hanna as in the question. Part (b) has no source solution; only part (a) is covered here.

solutions.latex:
Using the $z$-score formula,
$$z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$$
Substitute $z=-2$, $\mu=86$, $\sigma=4$.
$$\begin{aligned} -2 &= \dfrac{x - 86}{4} \\ x - 86 &= -8 \\ x &= 78 \end{aligned}$$
Hanna's actual mark was 78.
criteria: Uses the $z$-score formula with at least one correct value, or equivalent merit

6749.stem: The marks in a class test are normally distributed. The mean is 100 and the standard deviation is 10.

parts.latex: Jason's mark is 115. What is his $z$-score?
Mary has a $z$-score of 0. What mark did she achieve in the test?
What percentage of marks lie between 80 and 110?

solutions.latex:
Using $z=\dfrac{x-\mu}{\sigma}$:

$$\begin{aligned} z &= \dfrac{115-100}{10} \\ &= 1.5 \end{aligned}$$

meta.format_note: Rubric written by us (source had none).

solutions.latex:
$z=0$ means the mark equals the mean.

$$\therefore\ \text{Mary's mark is } 100$$

Find the $z$-scores of the two marks.
$$\begin{aligned} z_{110} &= \dfrac{110-100}{10} = 1 \\ z_{80} &= \dfrac{80-100}{10} = -2 \end{aligned}$$
So 110 is $+1\sigma$ and 80 is $-2\sigma$.

Using the 68% and 95% rules, the percentage between $-2\sigma$ and $+1\sigma$ is
$$\begin{aligned} 68+(95-68)\times\dfrac{1}{2} &= 81.5\% \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ 81.5\%$$
criteria: Identifies the $z$-scores $+1$ and $-2$, or equivalent merit

meta.format_note: Added z-score calculations to show where $+1\sigma$ and $-2\sigma$ come from; rubric written by us.

6787.stem: The assessment marks for a Biology assessment and a History assessment are both normally distributed. The Biology assessment has a mean of 74 and a standard deviation of 3. The History assessment has a mean of 82 and a standard deviation of 1.5.

parts.latex: Kathryn knows that her $z$-score for both her Biology assessment and History assessment are the same. She received a mark of 80 in Biology. Calculate her assessment mark for her history assessment.
What percentage of students received a lower score than Kathryn in her Biology assessment?

solutions.latex:
Find the $z$-score using $z = \dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}$.
$$z_{\text{Biology}} = \dfrac{80 - 74}{3} = 2$$
The History $z$-score is also $2$.
$$\begin{aligned} 2 &= \dfrac{x - 82}{1.5} \\ x - 82 &= 3 \\ x &= 85 \end{aligned}$$
$$\therefore\ \text{Kathryn's History mark is } 85$$
criteria: Finds the correct $z$-score for Biology, or finds an incorrect $z$-score but uses it correctly to find the History score, or equivalent merit

solutions.latex:
Kathryn's $z$-score is $2$, so her mark is $2$ standard deviations above the mean. By the $68$–$95$–$99.7$ rule, $95\%$ of scores lie within $2$ standard deviations, leaving $2.5\%$ above.
$$\therefore\ 97.5\%$$

meta.format_note: Added a short reason (empirical rule) for the 97.5%.
